title: How do the Old and New Testaments connect?
aliases: the old and new testaments connect question
the old and new testaments connect in the bible
the old and new testaments connect overview
summary: The New Testament connects itself to the Old by quoting, rereading, and claiming fulfillment of Israel’s Scriptures. In Luke 24, Jesus reads the Law, Prophets, and Psalms in light of his suffering and resurrection. Matthew says he comes to fulfill the Law and the Prophets; Paul says God’s promises find their “yes” in Christ. These are specific ways the New Testament writers describe continuity, while each passage still has its own setting and purpose.
historical_context: The New Testament writers treat Israel’s Scriptures as the shared textual memory of their communities. Luke 24 names the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms; 1 Peter 1 describes prophets whose words served later readers. These passages show the writers locating their claims about Jesus within earlier Scripture rather than presenting them as a story with no roots in Israel’s past.
ancient_near_east_context: The evidence for this connection in the cited passages is the New Testament’s own use of Scripture: Jesus interprets Israel’s writings, Paul invokes God’s promises, and Hebrews describes God speaking through the prophets and in the Son. That textual relationship can be explained without broad comparisons to other ancient collections or claims about them.
literary_context: The New Testament connects the Testaments through several visible practices: direct interpretation, quotation, and claims of fulfillment. Luke 24 shows Jesus interpreting Moses and the Prophets; Matthew 5 says he fulfills rather than abolishes; Romans 15 says earlier Scripture was written to instruct and encourage; 2 Corinthians 1 and Hebrews 1 connect God’s promises and speech with Christ. Not every passage makes the connection in the same way.
covenantal_significance: The cited passages present continuity and development together. Matthew 5 portrays Jesus as fulfilling the Law and the Prophets, while 2 Corinthians 1 says God’s promises are affirmed in him. Hebrews 1 describes a decisive new stage in how God speaks, and Luke 24 places Jesus’ suffering and resurrection within Israel’s Scriptures. The New Testament’s claim is that these earlier writings remain essential to understanding its message about Christ.
canonical_role: This question helps readers follow how the New Testament reads Israel’s Scriptures. Luke 24 provides a model of interpretation centered on Jesus’ suffering and resurrection; Romans 15 explains the earlier writings’ continuing role in instruction and hope; and 1 Peter 1 portrays prophetic words as serving later readers. The connections are made by particular texts and arguments, not by assuming every Old Testament passage says the same thing.
